chapters.summary: Chair Shirley Aldebol welcomes attendees to the second hearing in a series on the NYC municipal workforce, noting last month's session covered recruitment and today's focus is civil service retention strategies.
chapters.title: Chair Aldebol opens hearing on municipal workforce retention

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Good morning and welcome to today's hearing of the New York City Council's Committee on Civil Service and Labor.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I'm Council Member Shirley Aldebol, Chair of this committee.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Today we will be holding the second in a series of hearings about the New York City municipal workforce.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Last month we held an oversight hearing on municipal recruitment and pathways into the civil service, and today we will be focusing on civil service retention strategies.

chapters.summary: Aldebol calls municipal workers the backbone of the city and notes that over 32,000 individuals departed the city's workforce in fiscal year 2025, raising the question of what is driving attrition at such a pace.
chapters.title: Aldebol cites 32,000 departures from city workforce in FY2025

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: New York City's municipal workforce is the backbone of the city, and municipal workers provide vital services that keep New Yorkers safe and healthy and keep daily operations running smoothly.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Yet, in the 2025 fiscal year, over 32,000 individuals departed the city's workforce, begging the question of what factors are driving attrition at such a pace.

chapters.summary: Aldebol cites research showing employees seek work-life balance, career development, and competitive pay. DCAS exit surveys show resignations outpacing retirements, over a quarter citing lack of advancement, and 54% would consider leaving for more remote work flexibility.
chapters.title: Aldebol reviews exit survey findings on why employees leave

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Studies and reports from the Municipal Research and Services Center and the National League of Cities have found that key retention strategies for municipal workforces are not

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: so different from those in private sector.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Employees seek work-life balance, stability, career development, and advancement pathways, and competitive compensation and benefits.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Responses to DCAS's exit survey indicate that resignations are continuing to significantly outpace retirements,

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: and over a quarter of resigning employees cite a lack of career advancement opportunities as this main driver for leaving.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Moreover, when employees were asked to make recommendations for how to improve the employee experience, the most common requests were for increased pay,

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: improved communication and transparency from management to staff, and to address staffing vacancies to better distribute workload.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: It is also notable that 54% of respondents of the city's employee viewpoint survey indicated that they would consider taking a job elsewhere if it offered greater flexibility for remote work options.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Given that city employees have shared the specific factors that not only lead them to depart, but that could lead them to remain in civil service, this committee is interested to see what actions

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: the administration plans to take to reduce attrition and retain dedicated civil servants.

chapters.summary: Aldebol describes new city efforts including the Little Apple free child care center, an expanded Mayor's Scholarship program, and a labor-partnership task force on civil service modernization, while noting lengthy hiring timelines still frustrate recruitment.
chapters.title: Aldebol highlights Mamdani administration retention initiatives

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: The Mamdani administration has launched several initiatives that make working for the city more attractive and more sustainable, including Little Apple Free Child Care Center for city employees,

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: and an

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: expansion of the mayor's scholarship program for municipal workers.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: We were also glad to hear last week that Mayor Mamdani has formed a task force in partnership with organized labor

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: to make recommendations to the state on how to modernize the civil service and speed up the hiring process.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: As we heard last month, lengthy timelines at every step of the civil service hiring process, paired with procedures that haven't been updated in decades,

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: frustrate civil service hiring, and cost the city highly qualified potential employees who simply cannot wait around for a job.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: We are heartened by these endeavors and the seriousness with which this administration is taking civil service reform, and today we look forward to learning more about how we can work with this administration to ensure that the municipal workforce remains an attractive career path.

chapters.summary: Aldebol thanks senior legislative counsel Rie Ogasawara, Senior Policy Analyst Nina Rosenberg, Chief of Staff Sophia Brown, and her District 13 team, and recognizes Council Members Narcisse, Hudson, and Morano for attending.
chapters.title: Aldebol thanks committee staff and recognizes attending members

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Before we begin, I'd like to thank committee staff, senior legislative counsel, Rie,

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Ogasawara and Senior Policy Analyst Nina Rosenberg for their hard work in preparing for this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I'd also like to thank my Chief of Staff, Sophia Brown, and my whole District 13 team for the work that you do to serve our Bronx constituents.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: At this point, I would like to recognize that we have been joined by council members.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Narcisse and Councilmember Hudson.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Oh, I didn't see you were hiding.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Council Member Murano.

chapters.summary: Aldebol announces the committee will hear testimony from representatives of DCAS and the Office of Labor Relations and turns to committee counsel to administer the oath for the panel.
chapters.title: Aldebol calls DCAS and OLR representatives to testify

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So now we will hear testimony from representatives of DCAS and OLR.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I now turn to committee counsel to administer the oath for this panel.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We will now hear testimony from the administration.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Before we begin, I will administer the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff

utterances.speaker: Council Staff

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Katrina Porter, Deputy Commissioner and Chief Human Capital Officer at DCAS, introduces colleagues Katie Ann Otar and Dan Pollack, and describes DCAS's mission to make city government work for all New Yorkers, including its workforce.
chapters.title: DCAS Deputy Commissioner Katrina Porter introduces herself and panel

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Aldebar and members of the City's Council's Committee on Civil Service and Labor.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: My name is Katrina Porter, and I proudly serve as Deputy Commissioner and Chief Human Capital Officer at the Department of Administrative Services, more commonly known as DCAS.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: I'm joined today by my colleague, Katie Ann Otar, Assistant Commissioner for Workforce Operations at DCAS, and Dan Pollack, First Deputy Commissioner for the Office of Labor Relations.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We thank you all for inviting us to appear today and to speak on our efforts to bolster retention and support our city's workforce.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: At DCAS, our mission is to make city government work for all New Yorkers, and that includes ensuring that our municipal workforce knows that we are working for them too.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: When our city employees have access to resources that improve their quality of life, from child care to career development and advancement, all the way through retirement planning, we are fostering an environment where staff can grow,

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: grow their families, grow professionally, and grow even more committed to delivering for New Yorkers.

chapters.summary: Porter describes the opening of the Little Apple child care center at the David N. Dinkins Municipal Building, saying the program puts up to $20,000 back into the pockets of working municipal families.
chapters.title: Porter details Little Apple free child care center for city employees

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Just a few weeks into this administration, Mayor Mamdani announced the expansion of the city's first free child care center for municipal employees.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And within months, we cut the ribbon and opened the doors of the David N.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Dinkins Municipal Building for the first barrel of Little Apples.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: The Little Apple is a testament to the city's commitment to expanding access to free child care.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: As we all know, child care in New York City can be expensive.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Through this program, the city is putting up to $20,000 back into the pockets of working municipal families.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: The very families who are supporting government operations each day.

chapters.summary: Porter describes the expanded Mayor's Scholarship Graduate Program, a new undergraduate support pipeline, the NYC to Learn e-learning platform, and the citywide career account with designated career counselors under Local Law 75.
chapters.title: Porter outlines education and career advancement programs

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Part and parcel to our work to increase employee retention are our opportunities for educational and professional advancement, areas where we have been excited to expand in recent months.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: In March, we expanded our Mayor's Scholarship Graduate Program and launched the city's first undergraduate support pipeline for municipal employees.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: This expanded initiative now connects full-time city employees with opportunities to pursue associate, bachelor's, and graduate degrees.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: With this initiative, we are making education more attainable and affordable, supporting professional growth and strengthening the skills of our workforce.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We are also looking to build employee skills with our in-house platform, NYC to Learn, a user-friendly, comprehensive e-learning site that has expanded access to training and development resources for staff across the city.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Finally, in 2025, DCAS launched the citywide career account.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: While some agencies may have had their own program previously, citywide guidance was issued and DCAS helped agencies to launch standardized programming.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: As required by Local Law 75 of 2004, agencies are designating career counselors that provide employees who request assistance either in person or virtual sessions to help them on their career journey.

chapters.summary: Porter says the pension system and retirement planning classes, pension Q&As, pre-tax benefits, flexible spending accounts, and public service loan forgiveness help employees manage everyday costs and plan for the future.
chapters.title: Porter highlights pension, retirement planning, and financial benefits

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: In addition to efforts to increase staff training, supporting employees'financial well-being is another important component of retaining a strong municipal workforce.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: One of the biggest benefits to working for the city continues to be the pension system and our robust retirement planning resources that help employees understand their benefits.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Through our classes, seminars on retirement planning, pension Q&A, or just being able to talk to their agency's HR team, the city amplifies the incredible benefits available to employees.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: These classes and seminars complement a broader range of city benefits, from retirement savings plans, pre-tax communal benefits, and flexible spending accounts for eligible health and dependent care

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: expenses to public service loan forgiveness that helps employees manage everyday costs and plan for the future.

chapters.summary: Porter describes the first citywide employee viewpoint survey under Local Law 76, with over 16,000 respondents and 78% feeling respected, and the second-year exit survey report where 11 of 14 categories received mostly positive ratings.
chapters.title: Porter reports on employee viewpoint and exit surveys

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: With a workforce as vast as ours, building a culture across dozens of agencies can look very differently.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Our priority remains cultivating a citywide culture built on the principles of equity, inclusion, accessibility,

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: respect and excellence.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: As part of the activation of Local Law 76 of 2004, DCAS, 2024, excuse me, DCAS launched the first ever citywide employee viewpoint survey.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: This first of its kind effort was modeled after the federal government's similarly named survey and provides the city with important insights into employee sentiments around a variety of topics.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: With over 16,000 employees taking the voluntary survey, DCAS was able to learn about employee viewpoints around their work, management, work-life balance, modernization, and retention efforts.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: It was heartening to learn that the majority of employees who took the survey, nearly 78%, feel respected in their workplace.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: As we continue to foster a culture of inclusion and transparency, DCAS has also launched exit surveys and interviews.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Now in its second year, the fiscal year 25 report shows that employees overall have positive experiences in their workplace.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: 11 out of the 14 categories received mostly positive ratings, indicating that employees felt positive about their overall work experience.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: The top five categories were related to work environment, teamwork and collaboration, leadership and supervision, communication, and equity and inclusion.

chapters.summary: Porter highlights the Civil Service Modernization Advisory Committee with organized labor, free civil service exams for high school students and first-time test takers, the doubled Civil Service Pathway Fellowship, and the new Jobs NYC Center.
chapters.title: Porter touts recruitment efforts including free exams and Jobs NYC Center

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: While today's hearing is concentrated on retention strategies, it is important to highlight the strides we are making in recruitment.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Just last week, we announced alongside Mayor Mamdani,

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: that we are launching the first of its kind partnership with organized labor to speed up and modernize hiring for city jobs.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: The Civil Service Modernization Advisory Committee is actively working to develop in-house solutions and legislative fixes to improve the city's hiring system.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: This is in addition to the administration's progress in connecting New Yorkers with job opportunities, including removing financial barriers and making civil service exams free for New York City high school students and first-time test takers.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Moreover, this past August, DCAS doubled the Civil Service Pathway Fellowship.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Expanding a direct pathway from college to city government careers for 400 New Yorkers, and just last month, the mayor alongside New York City Small Business Services and DCAS opened the Jobs NYC Center,

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: a walk-in hub connecting New Yorkers to good-paying jobs in public service.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We are utilizing all the tools available to position the city of New York as an employer of choice.

chapters.summary: Porter says the city's 85% retention rate matches New York State and the federal government, that median city tenure is about nine years versus three in the private sector, and that the vacancy rate has fallen to 3.8% from 8.4% in 2021.
chapters.title: Porter presents retention and tenure data showing 85% retention rate

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: When looking at the data, we see that the city of New York is competitive with the private sector when it comes to filling vacancies with talented New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And our retention rate, 85%, is similar to other large public sector employers like New York State and the federal government, both at 85%.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: However, the data does not show the full picture of retention in municipal employment.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: If you want to measure the success of retention, a good indicator is the median tenure of employees.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: This can...

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: provide a more accurate picture of the city's retention efforts and success.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: DCAS data shows that compared to the three-year average time an employee stays in a private sector position, a city employee serves nearly three times as long, or about nine years.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: In fact, three-quarters of the workforce has served for five years or more.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Moreover, the city's vacancy rate overall is low, approximately 3.8%, down from a high of 8.4% in November of 2021.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: It is a reassuring sign that we continue to see very high rates for both retention and tenure.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We all know that retaining a strong, engaged, and diverse workforce is essential to delivering the services New Yorkers rely on every day.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We are driven by our commitment to strengthen the entire employee experience, from expanding access to government jobs to creating opportunities for growth, development, and advancement.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: By investing in our people and building a workplace where employees can see a future for themselves, we can ensure talented New Yorkers not only choose city government,

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: but trust that they can build a meaningful and lasting career here.

chapters.summary: Porter concludes that investing in employees ensures talented New Yorkers can build lasting careers with the city, thanks the committee, and notes Dan Pollack will also read testimony.
chapters.title: Porter closes testimony and hands off to OLR

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Thank you for your time and attention, and we're happy to answer any questions you may have.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And then I'm sorry, before we go for questions, Dan is also going to read.

chapters.summary: Daniel Pollack, First Deputy Commissioner at the Mayor's Office of Labor Relations, introduces colleague Zach Leiter, apologizes for a cold, and says he will outline collective bargaining efforts on recruitment and retention.
chapters.title: OLR First Deputy Commissioner Daniel Pollack introduces himself

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Aldeball and members of the Civil Service and Labor Committee.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: My name is Daniel Pollack.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: I'm the first deputy commissioner at the Mayor's Office of Labor Relations.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: I'm joined today by my colleague, Zach Leiter, associate commissioner at OLR.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: I'm going over a bit of a cold, so I ask that you would bear with me.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Today, I will outline our efforts to improve recruitment retention within the city workforce through the collective bargaining process.

chapters.summary: Pollack says the last round delivered over 16% wage increases over five years, a flexible work pilot extended through June 2027, and equity funding that raised entry pay, eliminated early steps, and funded retention bonuses for titles like lifeguards, 911 operators, and DSS caseworkers.
chapters.title: Pollack describes wage increases and equity funding in last bargaining round

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: In the last round of bargaining, when we were coming out of the COVID pandemic and the nationwide recruitment retention challenges, often referred to as the Great Resignation, recruitment and retention were really at the forefront of our focus.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: We delivered the most significant wage increases in more than a decade, totaling over 16% over five years for city workers.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Agreements also included our flexible work pilot, which was recently extended through June of 2027.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: And we also used a concept that we called equity funding to target specific titles with particularly concerning recruitment retention challenges.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: This equity funding was used for things such as increasing pay for entry-level roles, eliminating early steps in graduated pay plans, thereby accelerating employee advancement to higher steps and retention bonuses.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Specifically, this funding facilitated, among many other things, permanent lifeguard and 911 operator wage increases, short-term recruitment,

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: retention bonuses for DSS caseworkers, accelerated top pay schedules for special officers and school safety agents, and a new salary structure for probation officers.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: With many of our labor contracts expired or expiring in the coming months and year, we know we have a lot more work to do on this front and dealing with recruitment retention issues is one of our top priorities as we approach a new round of bargaining.

chapters.summary: Pollack describes OLR-administered benefits including health, deferred compensation, flexible spending accounts, IRAs, and union welfare funds, and highlights the new NICE PPO plan with an expanded retirement network and wider behavioral health network.
chapters.title: Pollack details employee benefits and new NICE PPO health plan

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Beyond wage increases, we always lean heavily on the quality of our benefits to drive up retention rates to keep talented professionals in city service.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Our office, OLR, administers a robust employee benefit program for city employees.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: It includes the health benefit program, deferred compensation plan, flexible spending account programs, which includes both health and dependent care accounts.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: New York City employee individual retirement accounts and the management benefits fund for non-union employees.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Unionized employees also enjoy access to union welfare funds for supplemental benefits like drugs, vision, and dental.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Many unions offer additional benefits through other funds such as child care, legal representation, and annuity, all of which are funded by city contributions.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: We are always striving to improve our benefits, especially our health benefits, most notably with the launch of the NICE PPO health plan earlier this year.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: That plan retains the premium-free, high-quality insurance our employees have enjoyed while providing significant improvements.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Those improvements include an expanded network for those employees in retirement.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: living out of state, an increased reimbursement schedule for out-of-network providers, and a wider behavioral health network.

chapters.summary: Pollack notes Work Well NYC's 10th anniversary and the employee assistance program providing physical, mental, and emotional health support, and acknowledges the city needs to improve how it communicates benefits to employees.
chapters.title: Pollack highlights Work Well NYC, EAP, and benefit communication gaps

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: In addition to the employee benefits program, we have programs like Work Well NYC, the city's workplace wellness program, which is celebrating its 10th anniversary this year, and our employee assistance program.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: We provide physical, mental, and emotional health support services that foster a resilient and supported workforce.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: We're investing directly in the daily well-being and work-life balance of our employees through these efforts.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: These programs provide a comprehensive safety net and financial wellness tools that set the city service apart.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: They're vital in attracting prospective candidates and giving current employees compelling reasons to build long-term careers with the city.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: One thing I'll mention is that we are always looking to improve the way we communicate out about our benefits.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: It's something we know we have more work on, and we will continue to make efforts to better communicate the value of our benefits to prospective employees, current employees, really everyone.

chapters.summary: Pollack says with many collective bargaining agreements expiring in the coming year, recruitment and retention will remain a critical point of discussion in the next round of bargaining with labor unions.
chapters.title: Pollack says retention will be central to upcoming bargaining

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: As we look ahead and with many of our collective bargaining agreements expiring in the coming year, recruitment and retention, as I mentioned, will remain a central critical point of discussion during the next round of bargaining.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: We look forward to discussing these issues with our labor unions across the bargaining table.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify, and I'm happy to take any questions.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I'm going to turn it over to Councilmember Hudson.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: She has to leave.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: She has a question.

chapters.summary: Council Member Crystal Hudson asks what percentage of the workforce the 16,000 survey respondents represent and what DCAS is doing to boost participation; Porter says the survey runs on a two-year cadence and the next is due in 2027.
chapters.title: Hudson asks DCAS about employee survey participation rate

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Just a quick question for you, Deputy Commissioner Porter, about...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: The survey, the voluntary employee survey, you said 16,000 employees took the survey.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Out of how many total, or do you know what percentage?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So the survey was released to all New York City employees.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We marketed the survey through agency personnel officers.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: I believe we went direct to the employee as well to provide them with the link and an opportunity to take the survey.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And that was the population that actually responded.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Do you know what percentage of the total workforce, the 16,000?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Employees are?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Oh, that's a good question.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Let's see if we have that.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And I guess while you do that, I'm also curious to know what efforts you're taking to get more participation in that survey.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So the survey is on a two-year cadence.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So we look at this as like the benchmark survey.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And so the next time that we have to administer the survey, we will try to do more marketing and get folks more excited about sharing their experience with us.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: But that should be in 27, right?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: The next survey?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And do you have a goal for how much participation you would like to see?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: If this is the benchmark?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So we're currently figuring out that statistics, and one of the things that we're looking at is the timeline that we release the survey.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: This is a survey that also goes out to the Department of Education.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And so within the law, we were required to release it by September.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We made some adjustments to make sure that we're able to get the teachers in, and so we're looking at the timeline.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: If there's an earlier timeline that we can issue the survey, that would allow us to have more opportunity to market it and to reach the entire population.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And so we're developing our strategies and thinking about that now, although the survey is not due until next year before September.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And, Councilmember, we can follow up with you on that percentage.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We don't have that available.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks the size of the total city workforce; Outar says 370,000 employees, later clarifying the survey went to 169,000 excluding DOE and H&H with about 10% responding, and promises to follow up with exact figures.
chapters.title: Hudson presses DCAS on total city workforce and response rate

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, what are the total number of city employees that would make up the entire universe?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So the total number of employees, sorry, I'll just pull that for you right now.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: Sorry, just got a couple of different reports.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So the survey was issued in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: The total number of employees that we have is 370,000.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: Yes, 370,000 employees.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And so the point in time may be slightly different in terms of the number of employee folks that were employed with the city at the time that the survey was released versus I'm looking at our tentative workforce profile report for fiscal year 2025.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So the numbers may be a little bit different.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And so based on that, we will see that the respondents would be roughly...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: It's like 4.3%?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: Exactly, around 23%, 25%.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So we'll definitely be able to get back to you in terms of an exact number.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We'll be able to look in our system to determine how many individuals received the survey and then how many people responded to it.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thanks, Chair.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks about the nine-year average length of service and whether DCAS has agency-level breakdowns; Outar says the workforce profile report covers citywide data and agencies can do deeper dives on specific titles.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about average employee tenure and agency breakdowns

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So the length of time that an employee has been in an agency, you said, is how long before they depart?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: The length of time for employees, the average length of time, is about nine years.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Nine years.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do you have a breakdown by agency in terms of the average length of service?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So with our workforce profile report that looks at the city's workforce as a whole, we're able to share the larger number and then agencies have the opportunity to go in and do a more deeper dive into what their agency population looks like, the title, demographics.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So there's an opportunity to go a little bit deeper.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: If you have a specific agency or a specific title that we're looking into, that's information that we can gather from an app application that we have that allows for that deeper dive.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Yeah, I think what I'm interested in is for those agencies that have a larger vacancy rate or higher turnover rate,

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: if people responded to the survey on those agencies, and if you have an average length of service for those agencies that seem to be...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Having difficulty retaining people and recruiting people.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And so the survey responses may be different across the board.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: One of the things that we encourage is that

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: all agencies share it with the departing employees.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: There are agencies and there are employees that have more responses versus others, but we don't right now have a direct correlation between the agencies with the highest retention rate and are they responding to the survey.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: That's information that we can definitely get back to you on.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Appreciate that.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks whether there are spikes in departures at three or five years; Outar says most departing employees leave within zero to four years, citing career development, salary, and work-life balance, and describes an information initiative on career pathways.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about milestones when employees are most likely to leave

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And do you see specific milestones after which employees are more likely to leave?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: For example, are there trends that show that there's a spike in departures as soon as an employee has been at the agency for three years, five years?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You said nine years is the average.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And do you have any idea what factors could drive those spikes or those periods of time when an employee decides, I've been here five years, I'm out?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So across the board, we're seeing that most employees are leaving.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: For the employees that are departing, it's between zero to four years.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And we're seeing the reasons could be different.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: If we look at the survey responses, most of them either cited career development,

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: larger than that and maybe looking at salary and benefits or work-life balance.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And so what that told us is overall, most people really do enjoy working for the city and want to work for the city.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: The fact that

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: career development is one of the things that pops up, lets us know that there is kind of an information

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: challenge that's there because the city, as you know, with our competitive titles, we have different pathways, there are different programs and opportunities for an employee, even if they're not interested

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: in staying in their specific agency, there's an opportunity for them to move across other agencies, maintain their benefits and, you know, time off and all of those things that goes with a city employee.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And so what we've been doing is really looking at ways that we can engage employees to share information about those pathways and about those benefits.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And so we have developed an information initiative where we're connecting with employees at different levels to share information about the programs that we have.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks how far out DCAS and agency heads anticipate supervisory vacancies; Porter describes the exam-based, data-driven annual workforce planning process with questionnaires to agencies and targeted hiring events for high-attrition titles.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks how DCAS does long-term workforce planning

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I'm going to pause.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Oh, they left.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Never mind.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Can you describe how DCAS undertakes long-term workforce planning for agencies?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: How far out do you and agency heads anticipate vacancies in a supervisory position?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Are there calculations that you make to try to ensure that as far as is practicable, institutional knowledge can be passed on to successors before an employee departs?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Okay, so the foundation of the workforce continues to be through examinations.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And so we partner with agencies at the beginning of each year and ahead of the incoming fiscal year to understand their immediate and future hiring needs to ensure that we're offering examinations to support their hiring.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So it starts out with a data-driven approach.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We look at active exams and other workforce data to determine a tentative list of titles that we plan to offer examinations for.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And then we provide that information to city agencies in addition to what we call a workforce planning questionnaire for them to communicate any changes or additions that should be added to the schedule.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And it's an iterative process.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: It goes on for almost five months.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And then we work with them to finalize the annual schedule.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: In addition to that, if they have like immediate hiring needs or if they see that they have titles where they may see high attrition and they need to hire up, then we take a more targeted approach through, you know, specialized hiring events.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Or amplifying their immediate hiring needs through our Office of Citywide Recruitment.

chapters.summary: Aldebol, drawing on her experience as a city caseworker, asks whether agencies have infrastructure to pass institutional knowledge to newer employees; Porter says succession planning happens at the agency level and DCAS does not manage it citywide.
chapters.title: Aldebol presses on passing institutional knowledge to new employees

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm just thinking, I guess I'm thinking of it differently in terms of your existing workforce

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: and whether, and this may be something that each city agency needs to think about, but

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Just passing on institutional knowledge to a newer workforce.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I was a caseworker at the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I had a great supervisor.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: There are things that you learn on the job that you don't get in an exam or, you know, the training that the city gives.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And there are people that have institutional knowledge about how their particular agency works or how to do the job, how to manage a workload that

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: is often not passed on to the next generation of employees.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I'm wondering if there is any thought to...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Creating an infrastructure in these agencies

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: so that people who are, you know, either have a lot of experience can pass on that knowledge to newer employees beyond the supervisory structure that may exist.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So I think that's a great question, and you're right.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: A lot of that does happen at the agency level.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: What I can share here is my experience at DCAS and, you know, our succession plan planning that happens where we develop policies and procedures

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: and ensure that, you know, that information is shared broadly across, you know, the line of service or the department.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: But I'm sure that at other agencies, they do have succession plannings.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Programs in place.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: It's just not like at a citywide level.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We don't manage that process.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Aldebol notes some NYC to Learn courses cost up to $1,900 and asks who pays; Outar says costs range from $150 to higher for certificate programs and are borne by agencies, not employees, and Pollack notes some union training funds.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks who pays for NYC to Learn training courses

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: What is the price range of the training courses?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: The New York City Learn website advertises several free courses, but we also saw some more intensive training courses that cost as much as $1,900.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do the employing agencies put the bill for these courses?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Are there any courses that are paid out of pocket by participating employees or their unions that you know of?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I don't know if OLR can answer that.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So our trainings, the cost of it can range from anywhere from $150 to, as you said, the higher end.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: If it's like a certificate program like Six Sigma, the good thing is that this cost is not to the employee.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: It is to the agency.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And so any employee that participates in our program are not paying out of pocket for those trainings.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And I'll just add that it's a fee-for-services model, so the city does not benefit from providing training.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: The cost is tied to the vendors that we utilize to perform the trainings.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: And to add to that, from the bargaining perspective, we do have some contracts that have reimbursement for training.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: We also have some unions that have training funds that the state contributes into that have their own training programs.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks whether DCAS tracks training requests and how workers learn courses are free; Outar describes outreach through agency personnel officers, training liaisons, dedicated NYC to Learn sessions, and flyers emphasizing no cost to employees.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about training outreach and awareness of free courses

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Does DCAS have access to information about the number of workers who submit requests for trainings and the number of workers whose requests are granted?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We can get back to you on the number of folks that have requested trainings, but for the number of people that have participated in trainings for individual users, we've seen that number has been increasing across the last three years.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We started out with about 13,000 that were engaged in training, and with some of the promotions that we've been doing in the newer system, that number has risen up to over 20,000 employees that are participating in training.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And what's your outreach to workers so that they know that this is available to them?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: At no cost, no out-of-pocket cost, right?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Because if I look at the website and I see $1,900, I'm likely to say, I can't afford that.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I'm not going to take her training class.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: Yes, and that is something that the team is very aggressive about.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We have, and, you know, based on the survey, we have seen that folks are not familiar with the information that's there.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So, one, we reach out to the agency personnel officers.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We communicate with the training liaisons.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We have now developed a training session specifically for NYCD Learn where we're reaching out to all of our contacts at the agencies, all of the employees who have engaged with us in any kind of professional development training to let them know directly that we're having this session.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We walk them through what they can get at NYCD Learn, how they can go.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: or through and apply, we also let them know that the courses are free.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We also include that information in when somebody go in to apply, we include that language that is at no cost to the employees.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And we also created a flyer that the agencies can share or place up with their employees.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So we noticed that as we were doing these sessions, a lot of employees were asking, you know, what's the fee to them?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And so we're consistently and constantly thinking about different ways that we can let them know that there's no cost to you, you should be engaged with this.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And we've seen that in the numbers of folks, more people that are registering for and taking the trainings.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks whether outreach has increased training participation; Outar says participation grew from about 13,000 to over 20,000 employees over three years, with classes filling up and more sessions added.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about training participation metrics

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Have you seen an increase in the number of employees taking trainings due to your outreach?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: What have been your metrics in terms of?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: Yeah, so that's what I previously cited where back about three years ago, we started at about 13,000 individual test takers.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And now we're, I'm sorry, folks that are taking our training.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So now we have about 20,000 people that are taking our training.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So we have seen a steady increase in that.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: What we're also seeing is that the classroom are filled and more people are asking for training.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So we're going back and including more classes to satisfy the needs of the employees.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks which course categories have the highest enrollment; Outar says demand varies, with Excel, project management, and leadership courses well attended, and DCAS does targeted outreach for under-enrolled courses.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks which training courses see highest demand

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And what category of courses see the highest enrollment or the highest demand?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So it varies.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We may see a course like Excel.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We have project management or our leadership courses are also well attended.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And so what we do if we see that there are courses where there may not be a lot of attention, we do direct outreach to certain populations to make sure that there's more engagement within those trainings.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And so we try to make sure that we have a wide array of trainings available.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks whether trainings lead to promotional opportunities and whether DCAS tracks agency participation; Outar says promotion outcomes are tracked at the agency level and DCAS data is not that granular, though it plans to engage low-participation agencies.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks whether trainings lead to promotions and agency tracking

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And do these trainings or some of these trainings lead to promotional opportunities?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: That information would be at the agency level, so we're not able to share that.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And does DCAS track data on which agencies have the highest participation in a specific type of training curriculum?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We are not that granular with the data.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We can and we are planning to look at how we can further engage agencies where we see a lower participation.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So one of the things that we do is we meet with the training liaisons now on a bimonthly basis, and we try to highlight the trainings that are available to them, encourage them to share that information with their employees, and we're looking at how we can reach directly to

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: agencies where we see little or no engagement with our training.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: That's definitely a part of our plan going forward.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do you know if the agencies are actually tracking that data to see if employees who participated in training programs are able to move into higher paying?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: Other agencies may have other retention and employee management goals, so they may track that.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We work with a lot of agencies who offer agencies.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: specific training, so they may have internal processes to track that, but I can't say for 100% sure which agencies.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I see you rejoined us.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I was going to call on you and you were gone.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I'm going to pause so Council Member Morano can ask questions.

chapters.summary: Council Member Frank Morano questions whether an 85% retention rate is worth celebrating given 32,000 departures, and asks whether the 3.8% vacancy rate accounts for eliminated or frozen positions; Porter defends the figures as comparable to other large employers.
chapters.title: Morano challenges DCAS on 85% retention and 3.8% vacancy rates

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Again, I'm still not used to a chair not going on for 45 minutes before giving other members a chance to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It's a tribute to your respect for your colleagues that you make an effort to include us.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you all for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Deputy Commissioner Porter, I was struck by something in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You point to an 85% employee retention rate and a vacancy rate of just 3.8%.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And you describe these as reassuring signs.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But the committee's report says more than 32,000 city employees left municipal service in fiscal year 2025 with resignations significantly outpacing retirement.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So here's my question.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Is an 85% retention rate something we should be celebrating, or does it mean we're losing roughly one out of every seven employees in a given year?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And when you cite that 3.8% vacancy rate, does that figure account for positions that it

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: agencies have eliminated, frozen, or simply decided not to fill.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Because you can make a vacancy rate look pretty good if you eliminate enough vacancies.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: That doesn't necessarily mean you've got enough people to do the work.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: To your first question, 85%, I don't know that we need to celebrate it, but I think that it is a good step in the right direction, and it is an indicator that city employees

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: are remaining in their jobs comparable to other large municipalities and even the federal government.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So I just, you know, we wanted to highlight it as a comparison.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Of course, there's always more work to do.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And, you know, just based on some of the programs and projects that have been recently

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: implemented and initiated, I think that is a good example of the city's commitment to ensure that we are retaining and attracting top talent and putting New York City in a position to be an employer of choice.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: As it relates to the vacancy rate, we use the data that was available to us.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: The idea of the state of affairs, if a position was eliminated or repurposed, that's not something that I'm able to speak to.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: But once again, it does appear to be a good, you know, an advancement from the heights of.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: the vacancy crisis in 2021.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And, you know, as we discussed the last time that we were here, it is also something that the city is committed to do, like figure out ways to attract top talent and to shorten the timeline,

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: you know, to get butts in the seat, to ensure that city agencies have the support that they need to, you know, provide service to New Yorkers.

chapters.summary: Morano asks whether agency commissioners are evaluated on retention rates and whether DCAS would support publishing agency retention rates with corrective action plans; Porter says she cannot speak to evaluations but is open to the discussion.
chapters.title: Morano asks whether commissioners are held accountable for retention

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Your testimony also talks extensively about management training, leadership, development, and improving workplace culture, and I think those things are all great.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But I have a more fundamental question.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Does the city evaluate agency commissioners and senior managers based on their employee retention rates?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If an agency is consistently losing experienced employees at a rate much higher than comparable agencies, is that reflected in the commissioner's performance evaluation?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I guess the question I'm asking is, is anybody held accountable?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Because in the private sector, if a manager keeps losing good employees, eventually someone starts asking questions about the manager.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Is city government doing the same thing?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So that's not something that I'm able to speak to here.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: What I can say is that DCAS, the agency, we're committed to supporting agencies and meeting their hiring needs through examinations, through professional development,

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: and in any way that we can.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Especially if an agency comes to us with a problem, a workforce problem, we're here to help them strategize and develop programs and opportunities to address their needs.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Do you think DCAS would support publishing retention rates for every agency and requiring agencies with unusually high turnover to develop corrective action plans?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So I think it's something that we can consider.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: You know, I wouldn't say here one way or another, but, you know, we would be open to the discussion.

chapters.summary: Morano notes the child care program has only 40 slots in lower Manhattan and asks how it helps workers in Staten Island or on overnight shifts; Porter says it is a pilot meant to develop a framework that could be expanded, and Hudson notes the long waiting list.
chapters.title: Morano questions accessibility of 40-slot Little Apple child care pilot

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Lastly, as a father of two, the points that you raised about child care really resonated with me.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And you spoke proudly about the new Little Apple Child Care Center.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But the city's new program has just 40 slots, all in a building in lower Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How many municipal employees have children who could potentially qualify for these 40 slots?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And how does this program help a sanitation worker in Staten Island or a correction officer working overnight or somebody whose job requires them to be at Queens at 6 o'clock in the morning?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I mean, don't get me wrong.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm glad we're helping these 40 families.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But I don't want us congratulating ourselves for creating a benefit that's inaccessible to the overwhelming majority of municipal workers.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Yes, point taken, right?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: However, this is a pilot program, and it is a step in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: to develop programs and opportunities for that, you know, will benefit city employees.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: The goal here was to develop a framework that could potentially be expanded.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: But right now we're in the middle of the pilot and, you know, we're more than happy to follow up and share with you, you know, any positive or not so positive outcomes from the pilot program.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: You must have a very long waiting list for that pilot.

chapters.summary: Aldebol notes the MMR cites a target of 10,377 training participants for FY26 and FY27, far below actual participation, and asks whether those targets have been adjusted.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about training targets in the Mayor's Management Report

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So I...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: What are your targets for training?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do you have any targets or goals for training?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: The MMR cites a target of 10,377 participants for both FY26 and FY27.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: The target is...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Much lower than the actual FY26 participation rate.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Have you adjusted those targets and

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: What are they?

chapters.summary: Outar corrects earlier testimony, saying the survey excluded DOE and H&H, was sent to 169,000 employees, and drew a 10% response rate.
chapters.title: Outar corrects employee survey response rate figures

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So I can speak a little bit about our goals towards training.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: But before I do, I just wanted to make a correction from the earlier question about the SADS and the response rate and the number of individuals that were issued the survey.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So the survey did not include DOE or H&H, which is included in our 370,000 numbers.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: They have their own survey that they do.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And so it was sent to 169,000 employees, and of that, 10% responded.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So I just wanted to correct that.

chapters.summary: Outar says DCAS is identifying additional vendors, building better pathways into HR and IT training, and expanding virtual, in-person, and asynchronous options in the spring catalog.
chapters.title: Outar outlines training goals and career pathway development

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: In terms of our training goals, we are, one of the things that...

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We do within the learning and development unit is a we're looking to see how can we make the training more accessible to individuals how can we collect feedback on what trainings what they're seeing what's working for them what's not and then looking at ways that we can engage other um

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: other sort of trainings that's where there's a gap so right now we're in the process of identifying additional vendors that we can use to provide more trainings to individuals so um for the

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: fall for the spring catalog that's coming up we're looking at how we can create better pathways into training.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So individuals who are maybe they're interested in taking on going into, let's say, HR path or an IT path, they'll have an idea in terms of what kinds of training they'll need to take in order to get there.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So we're really looking at, yes, we always want to increase.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We always want to make sure that we have, you know,

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: enough people that are aware of the trainings and are taking part in that, but we're also looking at the diversity of the training, the flexibility of the training.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: Are we offering virtual trainings, in-person trainings?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We're also looking into trainings where folks can be, it's more asynchronous, so they are not necessarily tied to a nine to five, well, being at the center for a nine to five.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks whether DCAS gets feedback from agencies on training needs; Outar describes listening sessions with vendors, agency partners, and employees, plus agency-specific supervisory training.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks how DCAS gathers agency training needs

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And do you also get feedback from the individual agencies as to what needs they have in terms of, you know, a trained workforce that they need to promote within or

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: move into certain positions?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: Yes, so one of the things that I did when we came into the role was do listening sessions with our vendors, with our agency partners, as well as the city employees, and kind of take into consideration what they were seeing and what they weren't seeing.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And so that has helped us to develop the additional trainings that we're adding to our catalog.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: Agencies also work with us to do agency-specific training, so that gives us a sense of where they're looking to train their employees.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: Most of them are focused on, you know, some of them have supervisory training.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: For the first part, they have a group of trainings that all supervisors must take.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And so we work with individual agencies based on what their needs are, whether they're looking to train only their employees or having more access to training on our, to different trainings on the platform.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks how promotional exam decisions differ from open competitive exams; Porter says DCAS uses data on employees eligible for promotion and can add exams to the schedule throughout the cycle.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks how promotional and open competitive exams are scheduled

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: On your promotional exams, the examination schedules published on DCAS's website show both promotional exams and open competitive exams that are scheduled for the upcoming fiscal year.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: How do the conversations surrounding an agency's promotional needs

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: differ from the considerations you need to make when scheduling open competitive examinations?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And what are the main factors that will weigh on the decision to schedule a promotional exam?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So like just going back to what I had described earlier about the collaborative effort, you know, the data driven approach that we take to the exam schedule.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: When we're engaging in that process, we look at.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Employees who would be eligible for promotion in a certain title.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: You know, you have to have like the permanent underlying title to be eligible to take a promotional exam.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And so we let that data kind of drive which exams we offer.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So if we see an uptick in folks being made eligible for a specific title, then we would ensure that a promotion exam is on the examination schedule for that title.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Are there ever situations where promotional exams are scheduled on an emergency basis?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We do have flexibility to add exams to the schedule throughout the cycle.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks how OMB's headcount budgeting influences promotional exam decisions; Porter says it does not, because exams are a forward-looking, preemptive measure ready six to nine months after administration.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks whether OMB headcount budgeting affects exam scheduling

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Given what we know about how OMB plays a significant role in budgeting headcount for agencies and how their process impacts the timeline for new hires, how does their process for budgeting headcount

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: influence your decision surrounding promotional exams?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: It does not because the exam schedule is a preemptive measure.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So if we're given exams during fiscal year 27, those exams won't be ready for use until six to nine months after they're administered.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So we don't allow that to weigh in on the titles that we add to the schedule.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: It's a forward look.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm going to pause.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Councilmember Felice has joined us on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do you have any questions, Councilmember?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Oh, he logged off.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Never mind.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I recognized him too late.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Okay, so I can keep on going.

chapters.summary: Aldebol cites Local Law 130 exit survey results showing compensation, benefits, work-life balance, and growth rated negatively, and asks whether agency organizational structures could add career ladder levels; Pollack says that is largely an agency prerogative.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about exit survey findings and career ladder structures

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Pursuant to Local Law 130 of 2023, DCAS was tasked with creating and distributing a comprehensive exit survey, which you spoke about.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: An interview protocol for departing city employees to understand the main impetus for people leaving the municipal workforce.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: In the most recent report reflecting survey results, a little over 32,000 employees left the city workforce.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And of the departing employees who completed the surveys, compensation, benefits, work-life balance, and growth and development were the main areas that were rated most negatively and were areas that were recommended for improvement.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Given the limitations on adjusting compensation and benefits, are there adjustments that can be made to organizational structures within agencies to increase the number of levels in the career ladder

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: and to provide additional opportunities for promotion?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: So as far as agency organizational structures, I think that would be the kind of prerogative of each agency.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Certainly, you know, to the extent OLR is involved in conversations with agencies about issues they're having, it's something we would often explore with them.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: There's also, you know, my colleagues at DCAST can speak to sometimes level assignment levels can be added to a job specification to kind of facilitate advancement within the title.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Those are a couple options.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
