utterances.text: In terms of changes to the organizational structure to kind of create more levels and more advancement, that's something that would happen at the agency level.

chapters.summary: Aldebol notes 80% of departures were resignations, 13.5% retirements, and 5.5% transfers, and asks whether transfer trends exist; Porter says movement is common given opportunities across 80-plus agencies.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about trends in transfers between city agencies

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: When looking at the data from the exit surveys and 80% were resignations,

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: 13.5% were retirement, and 5.5% were transfers to other city agencies,

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: have you identified any particular trends where employees from one agency are likely to transfer to another because the skills necessary are similar?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And there may be more opportunities for career development at the destination agency.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So I think it's common for employees to move around city government just based on the vast number of opportunities that may be available.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So it will be difficult to kind of like hone in on a specific reason.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: I think it's just more about, you know, the number of positions and opportunities that are available across the 80 plus agencies.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: With available vacancies.

chapters.summary: Aldebol cites survey data that 35% of employees found work-life balance skewed and felt emotionally drained; Outar and Pollack describe Work Well NYC, which reached over 60,000 participants, and the employee assistance program.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about work-life balance and employee wellness programs

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So in the survey, again, the most recent results of the survey,

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: it revealed that a large number of city employees, 35%, found work-life balance to be skewed and reported feeling emotionally drained.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Are there any initiatives that DCAS can implement or has implemented or can recommend to agencies to implement to improve work-life balance?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So I think work-life balance can show up in different ways across different titles.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: One of the things that, and Ola may be able to speak to this, is the Work Well program that provides a lot of different trainings and activities that individual and agencies can participate in, in terms of how to really engage their employees.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: I know internally within our agencies, our agency provide a lot of opportunities for us to kind of decompress.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We have a meditation room.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So agencies do a lot of different things based on the needs of their workforce.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And then there are citywide programs that OLR can speak about in terms of work well.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Gerald.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: So, yeah, I would highlight WorkWell NYC.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: So far this year, WorkWell has reached over 60,000 participants for its programming.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: So, you know, we launched that program 10 years ago for this reason.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: We know that addressing employee wellness, you know, there's more than just wages and traditional benefits.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Addressing wellness through fitness classes, through counseling, through things like that is so important.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: I'd also highlight the employee assistance program, which has been around longer, but is a vital resource for employees and agencies when employees are facing challenges.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: It's available for employees.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: It's available for their families.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: And there's a lot of value there in both.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Dealing with short-term issues, so someone who's experiencing mental health issues or

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: burnout or something can have a very kind of immediate appointment with a licensed clinical social worker.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: But we also work hard to connect people with providers that take our insurance.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: So one of the most valuable parts of EAP is they have relationships with our insurance providers, with our

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: with a lot of healthcare providers out there.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: And I know it's often hard for people to find appointments for mental health that take insurance.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: And EAP is a great resource there for employees to go.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: They'll get set up with someone who is accepting new patients, who is taking our insurance, and that can help with some of the mental health challenges employees face.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks whether managers are trained to remind employees about wellness programs; Pollack says OLR created a new communications division and acknowledges benefit communication needs improvement, while Outar notes stress and emotional intelligence courses.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks whether supervisors are trained to promote wellness programs

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do you know if managers, supervisors are, I guess, trained to...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Talk to their employees about these programs.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You know, I know that if we've had an especially tough week, you know, I remind my staff that these programs are available, you know, and

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: you know, it's almost a constant reminder because people will just keep plowing along and not think about it.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So I'm just wondering if that's something that you've incorporated or if you know that the agencies have incorporated that in their, you know, kind of like training.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Supervisory training

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: to remind people that these are available to them.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Yeah, I can just speak initially and then turn to my DCAS colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: So we work very closely with DCAS to provide information and work with them to get information out to agencies about these programs.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: As I mentioned in my testimony, I think we have at OLR identified that this is an area where we can improve communicating about our benefits.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: It's a hard city, a lot of employees, and we think there are a lot of people who probably don't have full knowledge of what we offer, and we can do better.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: So, you know, I'll tell you that we've...

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: OLR, newly this year, has a communications division.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: We never had a communications division before.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: And one of something that is very important is communicating these benefits out to our employees.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: So it's a priority for us to keep working at it.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: And I can let my D-TAS colleagues speak to some of their role.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We also offer a lot of trainings around managing stress, emotional intelligence, as a part of our training catalogs.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And we do, those are some of the classes that we always see a lot of folks that are engaged in.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So each year we try to make sure that we have different courses that can just address the employee's well-being as a part of our training catalog.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And I would also add that in general, managers or supervisors may refer their employees to the agency's HR department who are trained and knowledgeable about the programs that may be available to employees who may need, you know, outside.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: support.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks whether EAP numbers include DOE and H&H; Pollack says EAP serves DOE, H&H, and other agencies while uniformed agencies have their own programs, and clarifies Work Well reached 60,000 participants.
chapters.title: Aldebol and Pollack clarify EAP coverage and participation numbers

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Yeah, because 16, does that include the DOE and other employees, or is it just the 100 and...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: What was it, 160-something employees?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: So EAP serves the Department of Education and health and hospitals.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Some of the uniformed agencies have their own EAP programs, but our EAP program will never turn anyone away.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: But it does serve DOE and health and hospitals and NIH as well.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: WorkWell will also participate with every agency who wants to program it.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So we do have a lot of work to do.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You know, it's 370,000 employees, including H&H and DOE, and 16,000 have availed themselves.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Oh, I thought it was 60,000, 6-0.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: But still.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: That's a better number.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Right, better number.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Still, the point stands.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: We're always looking for ways to expand and to reach more people.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: And we certainly welcome the council's thoughts and partnership in any ideas you may have.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: But it's a constant effort.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Like I said, it's not different.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Types of employees you have to reach in different ways and something we're always working through.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks whether agency heads or the mayor's office decide which titles get hybrid work; Pollack says under agreements with DC 37 and other unions, agencies decide the degree of remote work and who is eligible.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks who decides hybrid and flexible work eligibility

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So as we talked about work-life balance and remote work,

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: is it the agency heads who decide whether a title is subject to hybrid or flexible work, or do these policy choices come from the mayor's office?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Pursuant to our agreement with DC 37 and other unions, it's the agency decides about the degree of remote work and who is eligible.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks about the comparative worth analysis required by Local Law 27; Porter says the city contracted with a vendor in 2025, desk audits are beginning, and the first report to the Council is due May 7.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about the Local Law 27 pay equity analysis timeline

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And as part of the city's mission to reduce pay disparities within the municipal workforce, the council passed several pieces of legislation requiring the administration to undergo a pay equity analysis.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: One such law, Local Law 27 of 2023, required DCAS to contract with a vendor

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: to undertake a comparative worth analysis of city titles with the goal of ensuring that employees across the municipal workforce who perform substantively similar tasks are paid similarly.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Has the vendor provided any updates to you about their findings?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And do you have a general understanding of the timeline for the completion of this analysis?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So yes, back in 2025, the city signed into a contract with illicit contracting to conduct that analysis and work is currently underway.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We're in the phase where the consultant will begin desk audits at the agency level.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And we're confident that and we're on track to ensure that that first report to the city council will be on time, which is May 7th.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So we're the first report is due to the city council on May 7th, and we're confident that we'll get it done by then.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks whether DCAS would review minimum qualifications for titles found substantially similar; Porter says the report will include recommendations and DCAS is open to Council input.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about a minimum qualifications review after pay equity analysis

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So after the results of this comparative worth analysis are published, are you open to completing a minimum qualifications review of the titles that the analysis identifies as being

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: substantially similar in work responsibilities, but which may have different eligibility requirements?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So as a part of that report, they will come with a set of recommendations and, of course, a dialogue with the city council on those recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So we're open to, you know, any thoughts or ideas you may have on that.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks about the child care waiting list and staff at the center; Porter says 37 families are waiting, and Outar says the center is vendor-managed with no city employees working there.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about child care waitlist and Little Apple staffing

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So we already talked about the child care facility, 40 slots.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You must have a very long waiting list.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: It's actually 37 families waiting on the wait list.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: 37 families waiting.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: How many staff are employed at the Little Apple Child Care Center?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: At their four classrooms in the facility, and what are their titles and roles?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So the Little Apple is actually managed by a vendor, so no city employees work at the center.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks whether departing employees can elaborate on personal reasons and whether parenting responsibilities factor into child care expansion; Outar says the survey does not probe personal reasons, though a separate needs survey informed the center's creation.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks whether exit surveys capture personal reasons for leaving

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Pursuant to local law 130 of 2023, DCAS has administered exit surveys, many cited personal reasons as their rationale for leaving civil service.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: In the survey, our respondents

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: that cite personal reasons as their reason for leaving, are they able to elaborate on the specific reason on the survey?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: If so, do parenting responsibilities come up frequently, and how does that factor into your decision to create this child care program and possibly expand it?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: The survey as it exists does not ask about for them to really go into what those personal reasons are.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So it's currently not being used to influence the child care process.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: I know there was a separate evaluation.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: survey process that was issued to employees to determine the needs of the service.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And so before the center was created, there was a lot of engagement with employees to determine what their needs were.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks about services at the Jobs NYC Center, which drew 2,400 applicants on opening day; Porter says SBS manages the center while DCAS supports with civil service exam information, kiosks, and a computerized testing center.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about Jobs NYC Center services and DCAS-SBS roles

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So the Jobs New York City office, I was there for the opening.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Very exciting.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: That has begun operations and we saw over 2,400 applicants who dropped by in search of a job on opening day.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: It's our understanding that the office focuses heavily on recruitment, which was our last hearing topic, but could you give us an overview of the services offered at this office, especially any programs that are dedicated to helping

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: current city employees develop professional skills or move upward in the municipal workforce.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And could you describe how DCAS and SBS divide the responsibilities of running this office?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Okay, so the Jobs NYC Center is managed by SBS, and DCAS plays a mostly supporting role.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So we're there to ensure that we can provide potential perspective.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Job applicants with information about the civil service process, about examinations and jobs.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: But mostly the center is managed by SBS and the model that they have in line is similar.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: to that of their Workforce One Center.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So they provide career services, they have workshops and trainings that are available, and employer services, job readiness opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And then in addition to that, they'll be working directly with city agencies to host hiring halls and agency spotlight events.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: But we're playing mostly a supportive role.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And what does that mean when you say supportive role?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Supportive role, you know, we're the experts in the civil service system.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We manage the examination process.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So we want to have a footprint there to ensure that folks who are visiting can, you know, have answers to their questions.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Are people able to go upstairs and take an exam if they're...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Qualified to do so?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Not on the spot, but we do have a CTAC, a computerized testing center in that building, so they could go upstairs for more information.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: But the goal is to have someone in the job center so that they don't have to do the back and forth.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: They can apply for exams at the job center.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We have set up exam kiosks where they can learn more about exams that are opening for filing and actually visit our websites and apply for exams online.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks whether the committee convened and what legislation could help; Porter says it has met twice, working groups are active, and recommendations are targeted for the end of the year, with an offer to brief the Council.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about the Civil Service Modernization Advisory Committee

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So on October 5th, the mayor convened a civil service modernization advisory committee comprised of city government

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: and labor leaders with the goal that the committee identify reform measures that the city and the state can implement to improve the hiring process.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the committee has convened yet and what the discussions have looked like so far and whether you think there is any legislation at the city level that would help further the goals of the task force?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: The committee has convened.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So far, we've had two meetings and conversations are ongoing about recommendations that we want to put forth by the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: My understanding is that, you know, we're more than open to meet with you separately to, you know, brief you and go more into detail about, you know, our vision for the committee.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: But things are moving along.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You have until the end of the year to...

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: The goal is to have recommendations set by the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: That's a quick timeline.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: I mean, so far we've met multiple times.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: There are working groups that are fully committed to getting this right.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And things are moving very quickly, but we're up for the challenge.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Yeah, I would really...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I think myself and probably other members of the committee would appreciate a briefing so that we can figure out ways that we can

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: legislatively move some of these processes along at the city level.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I know a lot of it has to go to the, some of it has to go to the state for, for those recommendations have to go to the state, but I think there are ways that city council can be helpful

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: to implement certain, certain programs or changes in recruitment or workforce development.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So, yeah, I look forward to that.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks how many employees enrolled in the expanded undergraduate scholarship program; Outar says about 91 individuals from roughly 21 agencies applied to schools, and DCAS is collecting award data.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about Mayor's Scholarship Program enrollment

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So the mayor's, I want to get into the mayor's scholarship program, and then I'll pause and see if Councilmember Narcisse has any questions.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: In March of 2026, the mayor and DCAS announced the mayor's scholarship program, which you spoke to in your testimony, which expanded the existing mayor's graduate scholarship program to include undergraduate degree programs.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: How many city employees have enrolled for scholarships for the undergraduate degree program since this announcement was made?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So I do want to clarify the process for the scholarship.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So one of the things that we do is we work with different schools who determine the scholarship amount that they would want to offer for individual applicants.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And so for the major scholarship program that we released, we had about 91 individuals from across, I think, about 21 agencies that submitted an application to the schools.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And then we're collecting the data on how many individuals received a scholarship award and the amount that they received.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks which agencies are most represented among scholarship seekers and how many applications the 2026 cohort received; Outar says she will follow up and that graduate applications are due in November.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks which agencies are represented in scholarship applications

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And what agencies are most commonly represented by employees who seek scholarships?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: I would have to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And since the cohort opened in 2026, how many applications have you received?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So for the 2026 cohort, that is for the Management Academy.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: I'm sorry, too many programs.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: For the graduate program, and they have until November to submit the applications.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So we don't have that data right now.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks whether DCAS is expanding scholarship partnerships with other schools; Outar describes cold calls, information sessions, and school resource fairs to connect employees with programs.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about expanding academic institution partnerships

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And are there any discussions to expand partnerships with other academic institutions to offer a scholarship program?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: Yes, one of the things that we're doing with both the graduate and undergraduate programs is to do extensive outreach to some of the schools that are not already participating.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And so we, the team does, you know, cold calls to reach out to different schools to really give them an overview.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We do information sessions to give an overview of the opportunity that's available.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And then once we have a selection of schools, we do what we call our school resource fairs.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So that way students can, employees can get a little bit more familiar with the programs that are available at the different schools.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So we try to make sure that there's a connection between the schools and the employees before application period closes.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks whether DCAS is coordinating with the state on high-demand fields for the expanding Reconnect programs; Porter says DCAS has not had that level of conversation but plans to share information with agencies.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about SUNY and CUNY Reconnect coordination

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So SUNY Reconnect and CUNY Reconnect programs provide funding to cover the full cost of tuition, fees, books, and supplies for people age 25 to 55 seeking to obtain a degree.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Is getting an expansion in 2027.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: It's getting an expansion in 2027.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: The Reconnect programs will now be offered to individuals who enroll for a degree in a high-demand field who already held a prior degree in a different field.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Are you in communication with the state for what career fields will be deemed high demand?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And do those career fields correspond to the agencies that have persistent vacancy or attrition issues?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So we haven't had that level of conversation with CUNY, but we have engaged with them in the past to share information with our agency personnel officer community so that these opportunities are shared broadly with city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We do plan to reach out to extend that offer for them to come and just share information in general about the program.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do you anticipate that current city employees will enroll in both Reconnect programs and the Mayor's Graduate Scholarship Program?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And have you considered staggering the timelines for applications to allow those who were not accepted into a Reconnect program to apply for the Mayor's Scholarship Program or vice versa?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Not sure if city employees are interested.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: However, we will make an effort to ensure that that information is shared broadly.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And then we can also think about the timing around the scholarship programs and deal with that on a case-by-case basis.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: But I think right now we want to focus on just amplifying the message across city government to ensure employees understand that this program is available to them.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks how DCAS gets the word out about programs; Porter describes monthly meetings with about 200 agency personnel officers, and Outar notes direct emails and information sessions for scholarship programs.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks how DCAS amplifies program information to employees

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And how are you amplifying those message across city agencies and how are you getting the word out?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Again, all of these programs sound wonderful, but if people don't know about them, they won't take advantage of them.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So we have a community.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: of HR professionals that we meet with on a monthly basis.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: They're called agency personnel officers.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: It's about 200 professionals from across city government representing all city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And we have programs like CUNY Reconnect come and present information and share resources at this meeting so that those APOs can then share that information with employees at their agency.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So that's just like high level how we help to amplify programs like CUNY Reconnect.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And I'll just, sorry, add in terms of like our graduate and scholarship programs, we send that information directly to the city employees.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So that way they're able to determine interest and then we host information sessions so they can ask more questions.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So we go through the APO pathway, but also try to get a direct path to the employees when possible.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I'm going to turn it over to Council Member Narcisse if you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you for being here.

chapters.summary: Council Member Mercedes Narcisse asks how much the city spends on overtime and why nurses, EMTs, and other health care workers are leaving; Porter and Outar say they do not have that data but will follow up.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about overtime spending and healthcare worker departures

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How much is the city spending on overtime hours?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: That is not information that we have available here.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because in 2024, the state controller reported an increase from 1.1 billion to 1.3.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So I just want to say the retention, and I'm so happy that you're working on retention, which is so important because we train people, we want to keep them, because it eventually costs you more money.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What does the data show, if you have it, about why city nurses, EMTs, and other health care workers are leaving and which agency we are losing them to?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: If you have it, that would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We don't currently have that particular information.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We can get back to you with the specifics of that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks whether DCAS has retention data on H&H workers and whether the city knows the cost of losing and replacing an employee; Outar says H&H runs its own survey, and Porter says the cost data is not available today.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about H&H retention data and cost of replacing employees

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: H&H is on the exit surveys agency list.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Does DCAS have any retention data on H&H workers, or is anyone collecting them the same way?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So for H&H, one of the, in terms of the cities and oversight, they participate in some of our initiatives and activities.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So for example, in our citywide employee viewpoint survey, they weren't included in that.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So that's one of the areas where they conduct their own survey and they're looking at their own initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So you don't have that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Does the city know what it costs to lose an employee and replace them, including recruitment, training, and overtime to cover the vacancies?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We do not have that today, but we can get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Narcisse notes most of the 32,000 departing employees did not complete exit surveys or interviews despite Local Law 130; Outar explains DCAS provides templates and guidance but participation is voluntary and subject to selection bias.
chapters.title: Narcisse presses on low exit survey and interview participation

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Over 32,000 employees left the city service in FY25, but the overwhelming majority did not conduct an exit survey or exit interview.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Local Law 130 requires agencies to offer both.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Why are so few departing employees being reached?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And which agencies are falling short?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: One of the things that DCAS is required to do is to provide the agencies with access to that survey.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So we created a template and issued to all of the agencies and their APOs so that way they can share it with their departing employees.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We also developed a template and a guide for the exit interviews and provided some guidance in person during our APO meetings for agencies and what they could do.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: Agencies, you know, at their behalf is responsible for sharing that with their individual employees.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: It is important to note that this is not a mandatory activity for employees.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: As their departing employees, we usually see also selection bias where they may opt into the survey process and may opt to share their feedback with us, but it's not something that they're mandated to do.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So the agencies just need to make sure that they have the access to provide the information.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: For me, if you get those information, you can actually find what's the problem and you can bring the solutions.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So I think those information are very important to share.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So at least we know what we're doing.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because like I said, we don't want to do penny-wise, dollar-foolish.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We want to make sure that when we train, we spend money.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I can give you an example because I've been a registrar going around and knows that there's

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: time that little things you can do extra to hold your staffing.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So you want to know why and how can we bring solution to the problems.

chapters.summary: Narcisse cites resignations rising from 71% of departures in FY24 to over 80% in FY25 and asks which agencies and titles are losing people and where they go; Outar cites social services and uniform titles and career growth concerns.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks which agencies and titles lose the most employees

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because I feel like I stay, I'm being honest, I went to Elmhurst Hospital for a few years.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I ended up staying there for 10 years because the environment, the things that they offer me, and the things that we get when we ask in the department, there's certain things that we need to know.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So at least we can keep our staffing in one place.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Resignations went from 71% of departure in FY24 to over 80% in FY25.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Which agencies and...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Titles are losing the most people.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And do you know where they are going?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Why are they leaving?

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: So the resignation may increase, and it depends on the titles.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: We may see resignation in some of our social services titles, some of our uniform titles.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: It varies based on the agencies.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: From our citywide exit survey, we can see that folks are leaving because they perceive that there isn't a path for career growth or some sites of personal reasons.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: Others may say that they are looking for compensation and benefits.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And so what we are looking to do in terms of reflection is to make sure that we're providing agencies and employees with information about how individuals can move throughout the civil service system and use it as a pathway for growth.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And also making sure that employees not only know that the process exists, but allowing them the space to engage with it.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: One of the things that we haven't spoken about is career counselors.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: Agencies, most agencies have career counselors who are meeting with their employees to talk through some of the opportunities to help guide them in terms of how they can look at other opportunities that are available to them.

utterances.speaker: Kadian Outar
utterances.text: And the goal is if an employee is moving to another agency for status plus, because we're still maintaining that knowledge, and we're still able to have that person that's serving the public.

chapters.summary: Narcisse thanks the panel and stresses that better data on why employees leave would let the city design solutions, warning against being penny-wise and dollar-foolish on training and retention.
chapters.title: Narcisse urges better data to diagnose turnover and retention

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I like the promoting within and pushing, I mean, promoting folks within the structure.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So at least they don't have to leave us totally.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And because we spend money to get people up to date to stay within our facilities.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So thank you for your leadership.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Continue doing it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But we need to be more active and more engaged to know why people are moving.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And those data can help us.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Give us the view of what's going on so we can bring the solutions.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So thank you, Madam Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Appreciate you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Hugo.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks how OLR and the administration identify titles for equity funding; Pollack says it draws on retention and recruitment data, agency conversations, and union negotiations, citing dozens of DC 37 titles plus probation officers and school safety agents.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks how OLR flags titles for equity funding

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Pollack, you mentioned in your testimony today that you, in the last round of bargaining, you used an equity funding concept to target specific titles,

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: particularly concerning recruitment and retention challenges.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: How does OLR and the administration flag titles to target with the equity funding concepts that you mentioned in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Is this based on recruitment and retention data, or is this also a conversation?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: With unions and other labor partners on their perspective on titles that need attention outside of pattern bargaining?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: It's not just one thing, it's many things.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: So it is, you know, we do look at data, retention data, recruitment info, we talk to the agencies, and we of course talk to unions across the bargaining table, you know, in the last round.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Engage with a union and there'd be kind of the question of, you know, is this a union that has a title or titles where this is warranted, this equity fund kind of concept.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: And, you know, it's a discussion we would have and we'd eventually, you know, reach an agreement that either did not include it.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: If we agreed there was an issue that

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: where it was warranted, we would include it.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: And it's something that we do with a lot of different unions.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Probably DC 37.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: We addressed, I would say, you know, dozens of titles through that process with DC 37, but other unions also had their probation officers.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: It helped facilitate their new salary schedule.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Special officers and school safety agents that change their salary schedule from seven steps to five steps.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: We really used it all over.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks where the equity funding concept is being applied now and whether contracts can be reopened mid-term; Pollack says last round's funds are spent, the concept will be considered in the next round, and reopeners are possible by mutual agreement.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about current equity funding and contract reopeners

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And where are you implementing this concept now?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Are you continuing to have conversations with the unions about where this could be best?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: applied?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: So for the last round, the units that had it, the money has been spent essentially, that process is over.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: It's certainly something as we approach the next round of bargaining that we will consider kind of how to approach those sales again, whether that concept should be included or a different concept with the same intentions.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: So definitely something we'll look at.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Is there a possibility of opening, having a re-opener?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Like, let's say you conclude bargaining and you've made decisions, but you find in the middle of a three- or four-year contract that there's a need.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Or a need is identified either by the union or by the agency, are you able to reopen bargaining or have a reopener to discuss the equity?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: You know, subject to mutual agreement, even though our contracts may have a provision that says, you know, neither party, as you're familiar with, shall make demands during the term of the contract, if we mutually agree that we want to reopen it to discuss a particular problem, we can.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Because there are a lot of questions, right?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: From others?

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks why certain employees are excluded from the NYC EAP; Pollack explains uniformed agencies like NYPD, DOC, sanitation, and fire run their own EAP programs with peer counselors, and OLR coordinates with them.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks why some employees are not covered by city EAP

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So on the OLR website, it indicates that EAPs are available to employees of non-uniformed agencies.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Can you describe the rationale for why certain city employees may not be covered by New York City EAP and what alternative options are available to them?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: So the reason they're not covered is because each uniformed agency has its own employee assistance program.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: So the NYPD has one, DOC, sanitation, fire, they all have their own programs with their own kind of infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: So we do coordinate with those programs and we'll assist them if we can provide assistance.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: There have at times been initiatives where we've worked with those agencies more closely and to help them out.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: It's not a matter of not wanting to serve those employees.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: We really want to serve anyone.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: But, you know, they essentially have their own infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: And a lot of the time, especially with the uniformed agencies, there's value in having someone who really understands that agency and that job.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: You know, for example, I think often they have like peer counselors who may be in the same title as that workforce.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: So that's kind of the background behind that.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks what factors shape salary schedules and how common retention bonuses are; Pollack says OLR weighs recruitment and retention data, where in a career employees leave, and union input, and is cautious about shifting pay between junior and senior employees.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks how salary schedules and retention bonuses are set

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: When OLR is negotiating with bargaining representatives, what factors are considered when developing salary schedules for specific titles and how commonly

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: are retention bonuses included within salary schedules?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: I would say when we're developing a salary schedule, you know, it's about priorities, right?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Whether it's a salary schedule or, you know, a longevity type payment, we have to consider how it would impact recruitment and retention.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Obviously, it's a very important factor.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: You know, we have to consider, sometimes we'll look at where our employees leaving in that title.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: If we see the problem is, you know, in the first year, we may have to put an entry salary and not be willing to say drop that down to elevate the more senior salary.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: If it's a title where people are leaving for some reason at year six or seven, maybe we need to provide a margin of longevity that can bump up the salary at that point.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: So it's nuanced.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: We always listen to the union, their view about what should happen.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: But obviously we are.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: also always interested in data about where there are issues.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: And, you know, for example, we wouldn't want to, something that often happens in bargaining has happened, is you drop the starting salary a little bit for new employees to fund something else, sometimes increases for more senior employees, something we've done before.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: You know, it's not always warranted, and sometimes it can be counterproductive.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: So we always want to make sure we're cautious of doing anything like that.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks how exit survey and interview data guide decisions to raise pay for specific titles; Pollack says OLR will review exit and viewpoint surveys, union input, and the year in which employees tend to leave a title.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks how exit survey data informs title pay adjustments

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So how are you looking at the exit surveys and the data from the exit surveys and the exit interviews to determine?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You know, what job titles might need a bump at a particular point in time or?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: We will certainly, as we approach the round, you know, review the exit surveys and the citywide viewpoint survey, but, you know, always want to be conscious of hearing from the unions about what they view the problems as, as a representative of their members, and we'd want to look at, you know,

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: We can look at where people are leaving.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: So if there's a title that we know has retention issues, we can look at what year people tend to leave.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Are they leaving in the first years or for some reason, which is more rare, are they leaving at 10 years?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And are you sharing that data with the unions?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: The exits data and the survey data?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Not directly, but the report is available on the DCAS website.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks whether OLR has a role in increasing awareness of DCAS programs; Pollack says DCAS does an excellent job promoting them, OLR will work with them and involve unions, and OLR will focus on its own benefit programs.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about OLR's role in raising employee awareness

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So you've discussed a wide range of programs administered by DCAS and other agencies that strive to provide city workers with unique resources and opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do you believe that OLR has a role to play in increasing employees'awareness of these?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And you mentioned you have a communications...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Department now and just want to hear more about that and what you see your role is in increasing employee awareness of these programs and

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: how do you carry out those responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: You know, regarding the programs you test, I think you test does an excellent job of promoting that.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: We will work with them, especially where, you know, it's helpful to get the unions involved.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: We'll often connect them, but they also have their own relationship with unions and can promote those.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: I think from the OLR perspective, you know, we want to certainly focus on the programs that we offer that we need to get the word out about.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks whether employees reliant on SNAP or CHIP can decline bonuses that might push them over income thresholds; Pollack says bonuses and salary payments are mandatory but OLR would consider such requests, and Aldebol concludes her questions.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks whether employees can opt out of bonuses affecting benefits

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: If a city employee is reliant on benefits like SNAP or CHIP, additional income can lead to such employees crossing the income threshold and making them

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: eligible for benefits while still experiencing financial hardship.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Are city employees given the option to opt in or opt out of receiving such bonuses if it will only exacerbate their financial insecurity?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: When we have a bonus or a salary payment, it's mandatory.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: I don't think we've encountered a situation where we've been asked whether an employee can waive it, whether a union or an agency.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: We'd certainly consider it if that happened.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm more concerned about like bonuses that might be a one-time payment that might temporarily knock them off, you know, eligibility.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: It's not a wage increase necessarily, which I find problematic.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So, yeah, it's good to know.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I think that concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you so much for participating in our hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you again.

chapters.summary: Aldebol opens the floor to public testimony, reminding attendees of decorum rules, the two-minute speaking limit, and how to submit written testimony within 72 hours.
chapters.title: Aldebol opens public testimony and states hearing rules

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I now open the floor to public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Before we begin, I remind members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant at Arms and wait for your name to be called.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Once you have been recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today's oversight topic of municipal retention.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony to the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony to the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: to testimony at council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Audio and video recordings will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: When you hear your name, please come up to the witness panel.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: For the first panel, we invite Rose Labaglio-Miller and Catherine Vaughn.

chapters.summary: Rose Lovaglio-Miller, Associate Director of District Council 37, introduces herself and notes her union represents more than 90,000 municipal workers providing essential city services.
chapters.title: DC 37's Rose Lovaglio-Miller begins public testimony

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: No, it's still morning.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Aldebar.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: My testimony, my written testimony has been submitted via email to you all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: I'm not going to read my testimony because I'm not very good at that.

chapters.summary: Lovaglio-Miller says the city focuses more on recruitment than retention, that many programs are unknown to employees, and that DC 37's 16.21% contract increases were outpaced by roughly 21% growth in metro-area prices.
chapters.title: Lovaglio-Miller says city programs go unused and wages lag inflation

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: But I do want to speak to retention in the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: District Council, oh, I apologize.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: My name is Rose Lovaglio-Mell.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: I'm the Associate Director of District Council 37 to the Executive Director, Henry Garrido.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: District Council 37 represents more than 90,000 municipal workers in the city of New York, which provide the essential services to the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: constituents in New York on a day-to-day basis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: What we've noticed in the retention of city employees is that the city does a lot in recruitment areas, not as much in retention areas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: And I know the city came up here and testified about all these different programs that they have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Some of them I've heard for the first time sitting here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: So, of course, that leads me to think about how are the employees in these agencies getting the information or are they getting the information?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: And I think they're very good programs that they're talking about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: However, they're not necessarily being utilized.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: I know they reach out to the HR departments of the agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Who the HR departments are giving that information to leaves a lot to be desired or understood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: There are also many other things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: I know the city also testified to our contract, our 2021 to 2026 contract, which we thought was a good contract where we negotiated 16.21% increases for our members,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: along with an equity panel, additional compensation fund, signing bonus, things of that magnitude.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: However,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: The prices in New York metropolitan area rose approximately 21% during that time, with rents going up, cost of food, utilities, and transportation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: So, you know, even though we may sit at the table to negotiate decent,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: good wage increases, it doesn't always translate over a five-year period when inflation and cost of living increases larger than the actual wage increase that you receive.

chapters.summary: Lovaglio-Miller describes members who are homeless or living in cars and calls for a municipal housing program, arguing that what the city deems affordable is out of reach for workers like school lunch helpers and park workers.
chapters.title: Lovaglio-Miller proposes a municipal housing program for city workers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: One other thing that I would also like to bring that actually isn't in my written testimony is we've also been trying to talk to the administration about municipal housing programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: One of the things that we find very difficult with our workforce is being able to afford rent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: In the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we have a lot of members that are actually homeless.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: And how can we try to get them out of shelters, some of them not even in shelters, living out of their cars, into a stable living environment?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: So we've been trying to talk to the city again about a municipal housing program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: You know, they talk about all these developments that come in and are doing residential housing and affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: My question to them is what is considered affordable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: What they deem affordable is not necessarily affordable to a city employee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: So we look across that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: District Council 37 represents titles from accountants to zookeepers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: We represent some of the highest paid workers, but we also represent some of the lowest paid workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: We represent school lunch helpers, city park workers that can't afford to live in what they call affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: So we would love for the city to turn some of their attention and looking at

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: at creating housing programs for the municipal workforce, especially since there's a residency requirement for the first two years for the majority of the jobs that they take.

chapters.summary: Lovaglio-Miller says the city could designate high-vacancy titles as hard to recruit, which would eliminate residency requirements and the 15% lower new-hire rate, tools she says the city is not using.
chapters.title: Lovaglio-Miller urges use of hard-to-recruit title designations

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: We also wanted to talk about the hard to recruit titles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: So the city of New York has the opportunity to deem titles that have large vacancies as hard to recruit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: There are some, there is a listing of hard to recruit titles already out there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: By deeming a title hard to recruit, it eliminates the residency requirement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: It can eliminate the new hire rate, that 15% lower salary for new hires that they have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: There's things that are at their disposal, tools that are at their disposal that they can utilize that they are not necessarily utilizing at this time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: I know they also spoke about the new DCAS advisory committee that the unions are a part of.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: I will say to you and submit to you that it's been interesting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: We have been having a lot of meetings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Some of the feel on the union side, though, is that the city already has an agenda and a plan of what it is they would like to do, and they're basically trying to get us to sign on to it.

chapters.summary: Lovaglio-Miller explains that non-competitive titles lack leave rights of competitive ones, opposes reclassification, and cites 911 operators as a retention problem where many recruits fail to complete training.
chapters.title: Lovaglio-Miller opposes reclassifying competitive titles as non-competitive

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: So when we talk about things like that and you talk about retention, we talk about competitive titles versus non-competitive titles, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: And just for the record, competitive titles take an exam.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Non-competitive titles are basically appointed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: The difference, and the city made a proposition about changing the classification and civil service status for a lot of these competitive titles to non-competitive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: However, the non-competitive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Non-competitive titles don't get the same rights as the competitive titles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Unfortunately, and for lack of a better term, we deem them almost like a second-class citizen, which is not something that you want to be in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: I could work for the city for 20 years in a competitive status.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: I'm entitled to certain leave rights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: As a non-competitive, I'm not entitled to those leave rights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: 3.5 slope things of that magnitude.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: So it's things like that that we think they should look at.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: One, we're not in favor of reclassifying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: We think that they need to be able to provide exams for the tests that are out there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: We have looked at, worked with them in job specifications and changing required qualifications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Some areas we agree and some we don't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: For example, a police communication technician, which we know is 911 operators, they would like to lower the requirements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Our position is we don't think that a high school graduate could be 17 years of age, might be at a maturity level to deal with some of the stressful situations as a 911 operator.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: How would we be able to support that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: The 911 operators is a perfect example of a retention issue that we have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: We can have 100 people apply to be in the class.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: By the end of that class, we're down to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: They don't even make it through the training academy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: So things like that, we think they need to just be a little bit more conscientious as to some of the requests that they're making in regard to how we change these specifications.

chapters.summary: Lovaglio-Miller says she wants to partner with the city rather than criticize it, urging the administration to use unions in a real, not superficial, way on retention and civil service reform.
chapters.title: Lovaglio-Miller calls for genuine partnership between city and unions

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: I mean, I could go on and on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: We could talk about the equity and salaries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: We could talk about wage reopeners that we do not currently participate in with the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: However, I really think my time here is not to bash the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: My time here is to really try to be a partner with them and for them to utilize the unions in a partnership in a real way, not a superficial way, because I think that is what will be best for all city constituents, employees,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: just everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Thank you.
