chapters.summary: Aldebol asks whether housing instability drives turnover; Lovaglio-Miller says yes, arguing that housing insecurity leads to discipline and resignations, and that municipal housing would be both a recruitment and retention tool.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks Lovaglio-Miller about housing instability and turnover

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I really, I appreciate your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do you believe that housing instability is a reason for high turnover in some of these titles?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: So unfortunately, I will say yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Because when you have employees that don't know where they're going to lay their head or they're worried about paying rent or, you know, so many other things are top of mind, you're not getting the best employee when they come into work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: So then that ends up leading to disciplinary problems and things of that magnitude where the city will actually, you know, we do have a lot of people that resign, but we also have people that they terminate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: So some.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: You know, not always because of their own power.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: So I think housing is a big part of it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: And I think if the city offers it as a city employee, that's an incentive for people to come work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: That will be a recruitment tool, but it will also be a retention tool because they know that they have somewhere to live.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: If I leave the city, I might not be eligible for this housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Thus, let me stay here because I have a place to live.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And I'd like to hear some of your ideas about the municipal housing program.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And we may not be able to discuss it at this hearing, but happy to sit down with you.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: As we have many times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: We have a housing program at DC 37 for our members specifically.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: So I would love to have the opportunity to sit with you and bring some of them in to express it even more.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Yeah, that would be great.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

chapters.summary: Catherine Vaughn, co-executive director of Abundance New York, praises DCAS progress but notes the Mayor's Management Report cited insufficient staffing about 20 times, and argues retention is a cost-effective lever.
chapters.title: Abundance New York's Catherine Vaughn testifies on retention

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Aldeball.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: Thank you so much for letting me testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: My name is Catherine Vaughn, and I'm the co-founder and co-executive director of Abundance New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: We applaud the progress that DCAS has made this year from faster exam results to the new Jobs NYC Center,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: but this year the Mayor's Management Report still cited insufficient staffing about 20 times as the reason why agencies fell short on other critical metrics from ambulance response times to inspections of our drinking water.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: Last month, this committee examined how the city recruits new public servants, and recruitment is one important lever to address the city's vacancies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: But as Rose just shared, retention is another, and it's often a more cost-effective one.

chapters.summary: Vaughn says 60% of employees who resigned in FY24 had less than five years of service, attrition is acute in frontline roles like ACS child protective specialists and DOB inspectors, and citywide overtime grew to $2.5 billion in 2025.
chapters.title: Vaughn presents data on early turnover and frontline attrition

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: The data points to two patterns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: First, that turnover happens early.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: In fiscal year 2024, 60% of city employees who resigned had been in city service for less than five years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: And then second, it's most acute in frontline roles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: In FY 2025, 295 child protective specialists resigned from ACS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: The Department of Buildings has reported 16% annual attrition among its inspectors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: Departing employees tell us why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: The top reason is career advancement, and only 29% rate their pay positively.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: When workers resign, agencies have to restart this costly cycle of recruiting, testing, training, and have overtime cover the gap in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: Citywide overtime grew from $1.66 billion in 2015 to $2.5 billion in 2015.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: 7.1 billion in 2025.

chapters.summary: Vaughn proposes automatic raises at six and 18 months, citing ACS as a model, and argues paying to retain costs less than replacing workers, noting FDNY EMTs top out under $60,000 while firefighters earn nearly double.
chapters.title: Vaughn proposes keeping workers through five years and paying to retain

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: We urge the committee to treat retention as one of the best investments the city can make, and we propose four priorities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: First, keep people through their first five years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: There are some examples that ACS has offered a model worth testing around providing automatic raises at six and 18 months, which is a critical window when a lot of people leave.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: And the city can measure whether these retention tools are working and expand the ones that do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: The second is recognizing that paying to retain workers costs less than paying to replace them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: This principle is borne out in functions like emergency medical services,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: You have FDNY EMTs topping out at less than $60,000 after five years, while firefighters are earning nearly double.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: So many EMTs leave for the firehouse or for similar jobs in the private sector.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: These departures are costly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: EMS union leaders estimate that training a new EMT costs roughly $42,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: And IBO found that EMS overtime rose more than 40% as attrition grew, with every 100 vacancies keeping about 27 ambulance tours off the street each day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: But investing in retention works.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: I noticed that you talked about 911 call operator, police communications technicians.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: When they won pay increases a few years ago, as well as overtime limits and compressed schedules, delayed calls fell by over 40%.

chapters.summary: Vaughn proposes planning for predictable retirements and promotions, and calls on DCAS to publish vacancy and attrition data by title and agency dashboards, plus a standing labor-management forum on civil service modernization.
chapters.title: Vaughn urges planning for departures and publishing workforce data

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: Our third proposal is to plan for departures before they happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: Many departures are predictable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: We know how much of the city's workforce is eligible for retirement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: And we also know about promotion schedules when there are promotional exams offered, for example, with EMTs promoting to the firehouse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: And then the final piece, you know, I was heartened to hear so many members of this committee ask great questions about the visibility and data around the workforce.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: The workplace assessments that this committee reviewed are a strong start, but they leave important gaps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: Fewer than half of departing employees offered the exit survey completed, and the survey asks why people leave, but they don't ask where they're going.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: And some of the most useful staffing metrics, like vacancies and attrition by title and time to hire by agency and title, are not in the mayor's management report or easily accessible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: So we urge DCAS to publish these statistics, including through creating agency dashboards that leaders can use to drive improvements and that also the public can use to hold the city accountable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: We encourage the city to pursue these reforms in partnership with its workforce and their unions, potentially through a standing labor management forum on civil service modernization that's kicked off with this committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: And we hope that you see us as a resource and partner in your efforts to retain our city's best and brightest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks what the Council can legislate, such as data dashboards; Vaughn says centralized data on where retention problems are worst would pay for itself, and Lovaglio-Miller agrees.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks witnesses what legislative solutions could help retention

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I have so many questions, but I feel like I can't ask them all today.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: But I think we do need to continue our conversations and discussions.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I think I'll ask the same question that I asked the last time when it came to recruitment.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: What legislative solutions can the city council

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: employ to make these improvements happen, whether it's data, creating a dashboard, mandating the creation of these dashboards?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do you have any ideas?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Either one of you can answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: I'll just, I can go quickly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: I think it's from the testimony that we heard today, it seems like a lot of these retention measures are really at the discretion of agencies, which I understand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: And every agency has to kind of run its own way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: So I do think that data is a place where if we had more centralized information, like there were many stats that you all asked for from DCAS that they weren't able to provide right now, or maybe they don't have access to because the agencies are holding that data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: And so I hate to ask for like collect more data, publish another report.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: I want to make sure that there's a good feedback loop.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: But I do think that if we knew like all these.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: questions about where are the retention issues the worst?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: Where are you seeing people leave?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: Are there managers, are there agencies, are there jobs where you're seeing people leaving so early and we're having to pay every single year to recruit and train new people and then they're leaving?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: I think that would, we would see that pay for itself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: The work to compile that data would allow us to make better decisions across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: So I think that's a place to start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: It's certainly not a place to finish, but I think that could be a good starting point.

chapters.summary: Lovaglio-Miller says advancement is slowed by lengthy OMB approvals to fill and place employees in lines, and that treatment of workers at job sites is an intangible driver of turnover.
chapters.title: Lovaglio-Miller describes OMB approval delays and workplace treatment issues

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: I agree with everything she said, the reports and stuff, you know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: However, I also say that a lot of it,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: It's hard to kind of put in words.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: It's the intangible, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: A lot of our older staff that are leaving, one, advancement, promotional opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: They feel like they get looked over.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Sometimes, even when you get promoted, the process that goes through, you have to wait.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: You've got to get OMB approval.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: So first, the agency has to reach out to OMB to get approval to fill a line.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Then they fill a line.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Then they got to reach back out to OMB to get approval to actually put the person in the line.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: It becomes a very lengthy process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: A lot of times what happens is people end up working in the capacity waiting for the approval.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: But when they get it, it doesn't go back to the day they started, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: So then that's when we have to end up like filing a grievance or something on their behalf.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: So I think that process can be streamlined.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: I know that is something that we're talking about in OMB swears.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: That they're willing to do it, but, you know, we'll see.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: So that's some of it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: And the other part of it that's an intangible is really just the treatment of workers at the work location.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Most people want to come in, do their job, go home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: They don't want to deal with a whole lot of drama.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: I mean, we have some that do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: But then, just being honest, but then...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: The way management deals with those individuals on the work location is also just a whole nother issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: So, yeah.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks how treatment can improve; Lovaglio-Miller describes DC 37's years-long effort to negotiate salaries for accreted managerial titles where pay ranges from $50,000 to $190,000 for similar work, urging a more streamlined floor. Aldebol thanks the witnesses.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks how workplace treatment can improve; Lovaglio-Miller cites pay disparities

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And how do you think that can be improved?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: So really, give you an example, District Council 37 accreted some managerial titles that are not doing necessarily managerial work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: We started this process in 2015.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: About 2015.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: We're still trying to negotiate salaries for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: So, and I'm saying to you, when the city hired them, they, some get $50,000, some get $190,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Like, that range is just ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And they're doing similar.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Yeah, it depends on what office you're in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: You know, I could work, three people could work for HRA, all have the same title, and all make varying, you know, salaries, depending maybe on the program or what have you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: As, you know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Unions, we never tell people to take money out of anybody's pocket.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: But what we are trying to do is raise that floor and have something more sustainable and streamlined where if I'm getting promoted into this title, I have an idea of what I'm making.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: It's not necessarily left up to the person that's hiring me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Things like that.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you again for your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And we'll definitely be following up with you on some of these questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Lovaglio-Miller
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

chapters.summary: Aldebol checks whether anyone on Zoom wishes to speak, then calls registered speakers Mamadou Juma Barry and Chowdhury Hassan Mahmood, who do not appear, and waits for the sergeant at arms to locate a sign-up.
chapters.title: Aldebol checks for Zoom speakers and calls registered witnesses

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I don't know if there's anybody on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: If there is anyone on Zoom, which I don't think there is, and wish to speak but have not yet had the opportunity to do so, please use the raise your hand function and our staff will unmute you.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: No worries on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I had two people register to speak today.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I'm going to call their names.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Mamadou Juma Barry and Chowdhury Hassan Mahmood.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Are they here or?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: No, I think he's going to get him.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: We're waiting on somebody who I think signed up to speak, but may have left the room.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I'm going to give the sergeant a minute to track down the person that signed up to speak.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Matthew Lee.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Yep, come up to the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Whenever you're ready.

chapters.summary: Matthew Lee, a legislative fellow for Council Member Narcisse, says early turnover and employees not knowing their benefits drive attrition, and proposes free transit access for all city employees as a tangible benefit.
chapters.title: Council fellow Matthew Lee testifies on benefits awareness and transit access

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: Awesome.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Matthew Lee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: I'm a legislative fellow actually for the council member Mercedes Narcisse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: This is also my first time speaking, so if I do break the quorum or any of the rules, I apologize.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: I'm taking it slow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: I wanted to talk about the testimony that I heard in this chamber and what I think might be a good direction for how to improve retention amongst municipal workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: The two biggest things that I've noticed, which we've had previous testimony point out, as well as

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: It's basically that turnover happens very early, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: The second thing that we also noticed is that employees

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: don't know their benefits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: As we talked about extensively, or rather you talked about extensively, with DCAS, right, there's a whole lot of effort in how do we educate current city employees on the benefits that they do have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: And I think that lack of knowledge

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: combined with jumping into the job early in those one to four years, as DCAS talked about, as well as previous testimony, reveals that that lack of knowledge on what is available to city employees

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: combined with the heavy work that we all do trying to help the city, makes it really difficult for them to stay invested in the job, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: And I think rather than simply thinking about it as just how do we get advancements in career and how do we get people to move up, we also...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: Think about maybe how do we get them to feel like they have those benefits regardless of whether they know about it, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: I mean, to the previous speaker and testimony's point regarding housing, that's something that regardless of whether you're making enough money or not,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: you feel the pressure of losing your housing more than you do the benefits that you are getting from the city at that point, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: And I think, you know, there's certainly many...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Have to wrap it up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: Appreciate you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: There are certainly many ways that this council can work on it, but I think even something simple like free transit access for all city employees would be a way in

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: making sure that if we are moving to change this city for the better, that we can move freely and we can feel that benefit without even having someone tell us, hey, you have this benefit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: Because it's as simple as just not even thinking about tapping the card anymore to get on the train or the bus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Lee
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Aldebol reminds the public they can submit written testimony within 72 hours, thanks the administration and public for attending, and adjourns the hearing.
chapters.title: Aldebol closes hearing and adjourns

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So everyone can submit written testimony at testimony at council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And we thank the administration and the public for attending this hearing to share their thoughts on this topic today and look forward to following up on these issues.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: With that, the hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Pollack
utterances.text: Thank you, Jared.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you.

summary: The Committee on Civil Service and Labor held an oversight hearing on municipal retention strategies, the second in a series on the city's workforce, chaired by Council Member Shirley Aldebol.

DCAS Deputy Commissioner Katrina Porter and OLR First Deputy Commissioner Daniel Pollack testified on child care, scholarships, training, benefits, and bargaining, citing an 85% retention rate and nine-year median tenure while acknowledging gaps in data and communication.

Council Members Hudson, Morano, and Narcisse questioned the administration on survey response rates, vacancy figures, exit survey participation, and accountability, and public witnesses from DC 37, Abundance New York, and a Council fellow urged housing support, better data, and free transit benefits.
